AbstractSolver
This class implements the operations of the org.smtlib.ISolver interface that map directly onto a single translated command sent to the solver process, with the expected response of a fully SMT-LIB compliant solver (a flat success/error/sat/unsat/ unknown/unsupported, or a bare value/attribute-pair for get-option/get-info): the command is translated with AbstractSolver.translate(INode) and sent via AbstractSolver.sendCommand(ICommand).

ISort.IFamily
This interface represents a new Sort symbol designating either a new Sort (if the arity is 0) or a new parameterized Sort family (if the arity is greater than 0); each new symbol has a (new) name and a non-negative arity.
ISort.IFcnSort
An interface to represent the Sort of a function; this is not something that can be written as a sort expression in SMT-LIB, but it is convenient to be able to represent the sorts of function ids uniformly with the sorts of other ids.
ISort.IParameter
The interface for a sort parameter, as used in sort abbreviations (including in the defining expression).

Solver_altergo
This class is a FIRST-PASS, CI-UNVERIFIED adapter for Alt-Ergo (2.6.3).
Solver_bitwuzla
This class is an adapter for Bitwuzla (bit-vectors, floating-point, arrays and uninterpreted functions -- no arithmetic logics, no datatypes).
Solver_cvc5
This class is an adapter for cvc5, on the assumption that it is (or should be) a fully SMT-LIB compliant solver: it is a concrete, silent inheritor of AbstractSolver — only the startup command line (cvc5 needs --incremental to accept push/pop at all, and --quiet to suppress informational stderr chatter that would otherwise fool SolverProcess's stdout/stderr-preference heuristic) and Solver_cvc5.start() (process lifecycle) are overridden.
Solver_simplify
The adapter that drives the Simplify solver.
Solver_simplify.Translator
 
Solver_smt
This class is an adapter that takes the SMT-LIB ASTs and translates them into SMT commands over a solver process speaking plain SMT-LIB, for a solver assumed to be fully SMT-LIB compliant.
Solver_smtinterpol
This class is an adapter for SMTInterpol (a Java SMT solver launched as java -jar smtinterpol-VERSION.jar, not a native executable): it is a concrete, silent inheritor of AbstractSolver -- the base launch command is declared in jsmtlib.properties via org.smtlib.solver_smtinterpol-2.5.command (see SMT.startSolver's %exec% placeholder substitution), so only the conditional timeout flag and Solver_smtinterpol.start()/AbstractSolver.exit() (process lifecycle) are handled here.
Solver_test
This class is a Solver implementation that simply type-checks formulae and checks that commands are used correctly; it does not do any proving.
Solver_yices2
This class is an adapter that takes the SMT-LIB ASTs and translates them into Z3 commands
Solver_z3_2_11
 
Solver_z3_4_3
This class is an adapter that takes the SMT-LIB ASTs and translates them into Z3 commands
Solver_z3_4_3_2
This is a special handler for Z3 4.3.2, as opposed to other revisions of Z3 4.3.
Solver_z3_recent
This class is an adapter for recent z3 versions (empirically verified against 4.8.12 and 4.10.2), on the assumption that they are (or should be) fully SMT-LIB compliant: it is a concrete, silent inheritor of AbstractSolver -- only the startup command line and Solver_z3_recent.start()/AbstractSolver.exit() (process lifecycle) are overridden.
SolverProcess
This class implements launching, writing to, and reading responses from a launched process (in particular, solver processes).
SolverProcess.NoResponseException
Thrown when a command gets literally no response from the solver -- either because the process was already confirmed dead before this command was even written (the pre-write liveness check in send()), or because its output stream closed while listening without ever producing anything on either stream (the forced-EOF check in listen()).
SolverProcess.ProverException
Wraps an exception thrown because of a failure in the prover
SolverProcess.StreamGobbler
Continuously drains one of the process's output streams (stdout or stderr) on a dedicated thread, so that a solver writing a large amount of text to one stream can never be blocked by the other stream's OS pipe buffer filling up while this process is busy reading elsewhere -- reading stdout and stderr sequentially in a single thread cannot make that guarantee.
